title: Proof by Mathematical Induction

findings.finding: The first induction demonstration uses algebraic fractions and extraction of a shared binomial factor without rehearsing either prerequisite.
findings.breakdown: Following the inductive step requires combining k(k+1)/2+(k+1) into one fraction and factorising its numerator. The preceding numerical investigations do not rehearse these transformations.
findings.checked: Checked p3-investigation-block, p3-key-ideas-block and p4-investigation. None rehearses combining algebraic fractions or extracting a shared binomial factor. The odd-n working in p4-d is an answer to an investigation, rather than a prerequisite review.
findings.assumptions: These are previously learned Stage 6 algebra skills. Calculator use does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Add three short review items before p3-investigation-block: (a) Write x/2+3 as one fraction. Answer: (x+6)/2. (b) Write a(a+2)/2+(a+2) as one fraction. Answer: [a(a+2)+2(a+2)]/2. (c) Factorise t(t+3)+2(t+3). Answer: (t+3)(t+2). Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse combining algebraic fractions and extracting a shared binomial factor before p5-induction-working.

findings.finding: p19-part-d repeats the complete sum-of-squares induction task in p8-q2-root without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The summands, formula and integer domain are unchanged, so the later task repeats the earlier proof.
findings.checked: Compared both complete supplied tasks: each asks for the sum of the first n squares, with right-hand side n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and positive-integer domain. No explicit instructional purpose for repeating the task is supplied.
findings.assumptions: Both tasks are assigned in booklet order; the positive-integer domain carries through the induction exercise.

repair.proposal: Replace p19-part-d with: “Prove by mathematical induction that 2(1²)+2(2²)+⋯+2n²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/3 for every integer n≥1.” Expected proof: at n=1 both sides equal 2. Assuming the k case, the next sum is k(k+1)(2k+1)/3+2(k+1)²=(k+1)[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)]/3=(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)/3, the required k+1 case. Conclude by induction.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy has different numerical coefficients and a correct corresponding identity and proof.

findings.finding: Extend the false-proof question to distinguish the inductive implication from the base case.
findings.breakdown: Changing the constant shows that a successful inductive implication does not determine whether the proposed identity is true.
findings.checked: For the offset −3, the assumed k case gives k²−3+2k+1=(k+1)²−3. For offset c, the n=1 case is 1=1+c, so c=0. These use the existing odd-number sum and the induction reasoning already taught. The short generalisation fits this Stage 6 course.
findings.assumptions: The extension follows the existing parts of p16-k.

repair.proposal: Append to p16-k: (iii) “Replace +2 by −3 in the proposed identity. Assuming it holds for n=k, prove it holds for n=k+1.” Expected: k²−3+(2k+1)=(k+1)²−3. (iv) “For 1+3+⋯+(2n−1)=n²+c, what value of c makes the base case n=1 true?” Answer: c=0.

findings.doneWhen: The two follow-up parts are appended with the stated expected answers.

findings.finding: The divisibility topic does not rehearse the index law used to expose the preceding power in its worked example.
findings.breakdown: The substitution of the induction hypothesis depends on recognising 4^{k+1}=4·4^k. Earlier supplied induction teaching and practice do not rehearse this power transformation.
findings.checked: Searched all supplied teaching and practice. Earlier sum proofs already use substitution, expansion and common-factor extraction, so those do not need another review here. No preceding supplied task rehearses rewriting a successor power. The index-law transformation is a substantial symbolic step, rather than a numerical calculation performed by a calculator.
findings.assumptions: Index laws are prior knowledge, consistent with the course library. Calculator use does not affect this symbolic step.

repair.proposal: Insert three short items before p30-method-block: “Write each expression as a multiple of the preceding power: (a) 5^{k+1}; (b) 3^{k+1}; (c) 2^{k+1}.” Answers: (a) 5·5^k; (b) 3·3^k; (c) 2·2^k. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse exposing the preceding power before the divisibility example.
